speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Mr Zhulkarnain’s question would not have come up for this Sitting.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Thus, we have to be careful on what we say in this House.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: I will, for my part, only set out the Government's policy positions, which has been stated publicly in the past.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The law, as it stands now, is based on current policy.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: This Parliament has also discussed the issue, most recently, during the Second Reading of the Misuse of Drugs (Amendment) Bill in 2023.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Why are the presumptions in drug cases necessary?

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: It is essentially to protect Singapore from drug trafficking.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The MDA presumptions deal with the practical challenges in proving certain facts that are often exclusively within the accused person's knowledge or which it would not be practical for the Prosecution to get direct evidence of.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: For example, the Prosecution will be able to prove that the drugs were in the accused person's possession.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: But it would be very easy for the accused to claim that he did not know they were drugs and by that way try and avoid conviction.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: And if he runs that defence, then it may not be easy for the Prosecution to rebut that claim or go get the necessary evidence to prove that the accused was indeed aware that they were drugs.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: For example, the evidence may be overseas and often quite elusive.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Therefore, the presumptions deal with the accused’s knowledge of the nature of the drugs.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The Prosecution must first prove beyond a reasonable doubt that the drugs were in the accused person’s possession.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: That will then trigger the presumption of knowledge.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Also, the Prosecution must still prove all the other elements of the offence beyond a reasonable doubt.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: These were the examples I gave, amongst several.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: First was, I quote what I then said: “A person was arrested at Woodlands Checkpoint.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: He said he travelled to Kuala Lumpur to look for job opportunities.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: He was introduced to a man known as 'Uncle'. 'Uncle' then passed him 10 packets of substances and taped these on to his body.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: This chap then claimed he asked 'Uncle' what they were for, but 'Uncle' showed him three fingers in reply.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: He was not aware of the contents and he came here.” And I went on to say how can the Prosecution rebut this?

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The truth is only in the person’s mind. “This is why our first Prime Minister, who was a lawyer, knew what the problems would be and reversed the onus of proof.” Let me give you another example, again, from the same speech: "  chap, convicted in 2008.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: He was asked by one 'Maren' to deliver items in Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: He was told that it was rare and expensive, that it was wrapped up so that it could not be spoilt by coming into contact with air.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: And so he went to Johor, met 'Maren' and brought it over.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Or do you think it is fair that the accused should prove it?” As I said, " e are dealing with lives here.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: But we are also dealing with thousands of Singaporean lives.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: And the person must get a fair trial.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Prosecution must prove what was the substance, how much was it, and possession, and any other evidence that they can find.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: If the person has a defence, it is only fair that he proves it." Sir, that was what I said here in 2017.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: That has been the position in law since 1973.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: While many other countries have faced huge difficulties in combating drugs, Singapore has been able to maintain one of the lowest rates of drug abuse in the world.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: That is despite the worsening global drug situation and our location at the doorstep of the Golden Triangle, one of the world’s leading areas for the production of illicit drugs.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: I went into detail on this just last year in my Ministerial Statement on Singapore’s national drug control policy.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The presumptions have been an essential part of the legal framework that enables us to deal effectively with the drug problem.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: We should be careful not to discuss the specifics of any challenge.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: And I believe the Minister of State for Home Affairs in March 2023, in his Second Reading speech, restated the Government's position on presumptions.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I did not hear anything new from the Minister, so I am trying to understand the reason why the Minister has to restate the position, because it is the existing position.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I looked at some earlier Parliamentary Questions that were filed.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In 2019, after the Court of Appeals judgment in Adili, there was a statement from the Government stating that it would be studying the observations made by the Court of Appeal and would set out its position in due course and as to whether any legislative amendments are necessary.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: This was with respect to the presumptions and specifically on the position of the Court of Appeal on wilful blindness.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: So, can I just confirm that the Government actually is continuing to review that particular judgment from the Court of Appeal?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Because that is the closest I think we have come to the Government saying that it is reviewing something on presumptions, but I am not sure whether that is the case that the Minister is referring to.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: No, that is not the case that I was referring to.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I assume that Mr Zhulkarnain's question arose because there is now pending a challenge in the Court of Appeal.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I would not go into that particular case and indeed, the question was precipitated by the recent constitutionality challenge.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: First, the landscape of drug abuse and habits would change.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I think the MDA sets out certain fixed thresholds for presumptions.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The second question is on section 33B(1) of the MDA, which requires: first, the offender's role to be limited to that of a courier; second, a certificate to be issued by the Public Prosecutor confirming the offenders' substantive assistance in disrupting drug trafficking activities.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: There have been a few successes, and our view is we are better off having it rather than not having it.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: That does not mean that a lot of cases get solved in that way, but there is now an incentive for the drug traffickers or the people persons who are apprehended with drugs on them, and both to show that they are both pure couriers, but also to give as much information as they can.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It puts more difficulties on the part of the criminal organisation or people higher up in the chain.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: That itself is helpful, as long as we see it in context.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: The Clerk will now proceed to read the Orders of the Day.
